"Fitting a model" sounds like a single act. It is really a search. The algorithm scores
how wrong the model currently is, changes the parameters to make that score a little
smaller, and repeats until further changes stop helping. The four pages in this section
take that loop apart, on the same simulated survey as the rest of the course:

- **loss functions**, the score being made smaller, and how squared and absolute error
  draw different lines through the same stations;
- **finding the parameters**, by a formula for a few models and by a search for the
  rest, and how to tell whether a search finished;
- **gradient descent**, the simplest search, and why the units of the inputs decide how
  long it takes;
- **likelihood and priors**, where each loss and penalty comes from: name the
  distribution behind the data and the loss follows, add a belief about the size of the
  coefficients and the penalty follows.

The section also pays back debts from earlier ones.
[Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) asked you to
standardise inputs without giving the full reason, and
[Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd) supplies it.
[Linear and polynomial regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd)
predicted a negative count, and [Likelihood and priors](likelihood-and-priors.qmd) shows
that squared error assumes a Normal outcome, which allows one. The same page shows that
the penalty [5 · Generalisation and model complexity](../05-generalisation/index.qmd)
uses to stop models overfitting is a prior.

- [Stochastic gradient descent](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/sgd.html), scikit-learn user guide. Includes practical tips on why these methods need standardised inputs, the point [Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd) makes on the survey.
